title: Troubleshooting a Network
sub: Find the broken layer in five minutes, fix it, and build netdoctor.zsh to do the walking for you
goals: Walk the stack bottom-up (link, address, gateway, internet, DNS, transport, application) with one command per layer
Recognize the common failure signatures from their exact output
Apply the right fix and know which fixes need sudo and which are risky
Split a slow request into DNS, TCP, TLS and server time with curl -w
Extend netcheck.zsh into netdoctor.zsh, which stops at the first broken layer and suggests a fix

blocks.text: "The internet is down" is not a diagnosis. It is a symptom that could come from a dead Wi-Fi radio, a missed DHCP lease, a wrong gateway, a resolver that never answers, a firewall eating port 443, a certificate that expired yesterday or a server that is merely slow. Every tool in the last seven chapters examines one of those layers. This chapter turns them into a method: test the layers in a fixed order, stop at the first one that fails, and fix only that. You will finish by extending `netcheck.zsh` into `netdoctor.zsh`, a script that does the walk and prints a suggested fix.

Have a Terminal open and keep your Wi-Fi switch within reach. Several exercises below break something small and reversible on purpose (a DNS server entry, the Wi-Fi radio), because you only trust a diagnostic once you have watched it catch a known fault. Everything that changes system state carries a `WARN` and a way back.
The layered method

Network problems have a useful property: layers depend on the ones below them. DNS cannot work without an IP path, an IP path cannot work without an address, and an address cannot work without a link. A failure low in the stack makes every test above it fail too, which is why random poking wastes time. The fix is a fixed order.
There are three ways to choose the order:

items.text: **Bottom-up.** Start at the link and climb until something fails. Best when you know nothing, and the default in this chapter.
**Top-down.** Start with the failing application and descend. Best when one site is broken and everything else works: `curl -v` the site first.
**Divide and conquer.** Test the middle (can you ping `1.1.1.1`?) and move up or down depending on the answer. Fastest for experienced people, and it is what the `trouble` flowchart below does.

blocks.code:
layer               question                         one command
  ─────────────────   ──────────────────────────────   ─────────────────────────────────
  7 application       does the service answer?          curl -sv https://example.com
  4 transport         can I open the TCP port?          nc -vz -w 5 example.com 443
  - name resolution   does the name become an IP?       dig +short example.com
  3 internet          can I reach a far IP by number?   ping -c 3 1.1.1.1
  3 gateway           can I reach my router?            ping -c 3 $(route -n get default ...)
  3 address           do I have a real IP address?      ipconfig getifaddr en0
  1-2 link            is the interface up and joined?   ifconfig en0 | grep status
        ▲
        └── test in this order, bottom first; the first failure is where you work

blocks.text: The rule that makes this efficient: **the first failing test is the problem, and everything above it is noise until it is fixed.** If you cannot ping the gateway, DNS errors tell you nothing.

blocks.title: Why ping an IP before a name

blocks.text: `ping 1.1.1.1` uses no DNS, so it separates "no path to the internet" from "no name resolution". If the number works and the name fails, the IP layer is healthy and you can stop looking at cables, routers and Wi-Fi. That single comparison removes half the stack from suspicion.
Layer by layer, with good and bad output
Run each command on a healthy network first. Knowing what *good* looks like is worth more than memorizing the failures, because anything that deviates from it is suspect.
Link: is the interface up and joined?

blocks.code:
$ networksetup -listallhardwareports | grep -A1 'Wi-Fi'
Hardware Port: Wi-Fi
Device: en0
$ ifconfig en0 | grep -E 'status|inet '
	inet 192.168.1.23 netmask 0xffffff00 broadcast 192.168.1.255
	status: active

blocks.text: `status: active` means the interface has a link (associated with an access point, or a cable with carrier). `status: inactive` means no link at all: Wi-Fi is off or not joined, or the cable or dongle is dead. If the Wi-Fi radio is off, `networksetup -getairportpower en0` prints `Wi-Fi Power (en0): Off`.

Since macOS 14.4 Apple restricts the network name for command-line tools. `networksetup -getairportnetwork en0` can report that you are not associated, and `wdutil info` can print `redacted` for the SSID, even while you are connected. Judge the link by `status: active` plus a valid IP address, and use the menu bar to see the network name.
Address: do you have a real IPv4 address?

blocks.code:
$ ipconfig getifaddr en0
192.168.1.23
$ ipconfig getifaddr en0
169.254.87.201

blocks.text: The first is a lease from your router's DHCP server. The second, in `169.254.0.0/16`, is a **link-local** address macOS invented for itself after DHCP got no answer (see [Addressing](#addressing)). It proves the link works and DHCP does not. An empty reply means the interface has no IPv4 address at all.
Gateway: can you reach the router?

blocks.code:
$ route -n get default
   route to: default
destination: default
       mask: default
    gateway: 192.168.1.1
  interface: en0
      flags: <UP,GATEWAY,DONE,STATIC,PRCLONING,GLOBAL>
$ ping -c 3 192.168.1.1
PING 192.168.1.1 (192.168.1.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=64 time=2.481 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=2.130 ms
64 bytes from 192.168.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=3.774 ms

--- 192.168.1.1 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 2.130/2.795/3.774/0.707 ms

blocks.text: Good: a default route through the interface you expect, replies in a few milliseconds, 0% loss. Bad outputs you will meet:

head: Output
Meaning
Next step
rows: `route: writing to routing socket: not in table`
the address step failed or the service is disabled
the Mac cannot resolve the gateway's MAC (ARP fails)
check `arp -an`; the gateway is down or you are on the wrong network
wrong gateway, router overloaded, or the router drops ICMP
weak Wi-Fi signal, interference, a bad cable

blocks.text: Internet by number: can you reach a far address?

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 3 1.1.1.1
PING 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1): 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=0 ttl=58 time=11.842 ms
64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=58 time=12.310 ms
64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=58 time=11.907 ms

--- 1.1.1.1 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.842/12.020/12.310/0.207 ms

blocks.text: If the gateway answers and `1.1.1.1` does not, the fault is beyond your router: the modem, the ISP, or an upstream outage. Check the router's status page and try `traceroute -n 1.1.1.1` to see where the replies stop ([Reachability](#net-reach)). Some networks block ICMP while allowing web traffic, so a failed ping with a working `curl http://1.1.1.1` is not an outage.
Name resolution: does the name become an address?

blocks.code:
$ dig +short example.com
93.184.216.34
$ dig example.com | grep -E 'status|Query time|SERVER'
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 31870
;; Query time: 31 msec
;; SERVER: 192.168.1.1#53(192.168.1.1)

blocks.text: Three different failures hide behind "DNS is broken", and the header distinguishes them:

head: You see
Meaning
Where to look
rows: the name does not exist (typo, or an expired domain)
spelling; try another resolver to rule out a hijacking one
the resolver tried and failed (upstream or DNSSEC problem)
resolver down, or UDP port 53 blocked

blocks.text: The decisive test is to ask a different resolver directly: `dig +short @1.1.1.1 example.com`. If that works and the default fails, your configured DNS server is the problem, not the internet.

blocks.title: dig does not use the system resolver

blocks.text: `dig` sends its own query straight to a nameserver. It ignores `/etc/hosts`, search domains, per-domain resolvers set by a VPN, and the cache. Browsers, `ping` and `curl` go through the macOS resolver instead. So "dig works but the browser does not" is a real and common situation. Test the path apps use with `dscacheutil -q host -a name example.com`, and inspect it with `scutil --dns` ([DNS](#dns)).
Transport: can you open the port?

blocks.code:
$ nc -vz -w 5 example.com 443
Connection to example.com port 443 [tcp/https] succeeded!
$ nc -vz -w 5 example.com 8443
nc: connectx to example.com port 8443 (tcp) failed: Operation timed out

blocks.text: A successful TCP handshake proves the path and the listener. `Connection refused` comes back instantly: the host answered with a reset, so nothing is listening on that port. `Operation timed out` means packets vanished: a firewall silently dropping them, or a dead host. Telling "refused" from "timed out" is one of the most useful distinctions in the whole subject; [Ports](#ports) explains why.
Application: does the service answer correctly?

blocks.code:
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://example.com
200
$ curl -sS -o /dev/null https://expired.badssl.com/
curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired

blocks.text: curl's exit status and message name the layer: `(6)` could not resolve, `(7)` could not connect, `(28)` timed out, `(35)` or `(60)` TLS handshake or certificate problem, and any HTTP status is a server answer (a 5xx is the server's problem, not yours). The full table is in [HTTP and the web](#http).
Reading the pieces of a diagnosis command

tokens.exp: the DNS query tool; talks to a nameserver itself, not through macOS
wait at most 2 seconds for each try
send the query once, do not retry
the server to ask, bypassing your configured resolver
one probe is enough for a yes/no answer
set the Don't Fragment bit, so oversized packets are dropped, not split
a far-away target whose path you want to test

blocks.text: The five-minute diagnosis
Put the ladder in one pasteable block. Run it top to bottom and read the first line that looks wrong.

blocks.code:
iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}'); echo "iface: ${iface:-NONE}"
ifconfig ${iface:-en0} 2>/dev/null | awk '/status:/ {print "link:", $2}'
ipconfig getifaddr ${iface:-en0}
gw=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}'); ping -c 3 -t 5 $gw
ping -c 3 -t 5 1.1.1.1
dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 example.com
nc -vz -w 5 example.com 443
curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 8 -w 'http %{http_code} in %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com

blocks.text: Seven commands, one per layer, about ten seconds on a healthy network and about forty on a broken one because each failure waits for its timeout. When a test hangs, [[Ctrl+C]] it: a hang is an answer too.
The flowchart above is the same method as a decision tree. Click through it with the symptom you are chasing, then confirm each branch with the command named on the node.

blocks.title: Change one thing at a time

blocks.text: After each fix, rerun the test that failed. If you change DNS servers and restart Wi-Fi and reboot the router in one go and it starts working, you have learned nothing for next time. Apply the smallest fix for the failing layer, retest, and only then go on.
Failure signatures
These are the patterns that account for most home and small-office trouble. Each has a fingerprint (the output) and a cause.
A 169.254.x.x address

`ipconfig getifaddr en0` prints `169.254.87.201`. DHCP got no reply: the router's DHCP server is off, its lease pool is full, or the link drops frames. Fix: renew the lease (see [Fixes](#fixes)), then look at the router. `ipconfig getpacket en0` shows the last DHCP reply when there was one.
Gateway unreachable

You have a good address but `ping` to the gateway times out. Check that the gateway is what you expect (`route -n get default`). A stale gateway after changing networks, a wrong static IP or subnet mask, or an access point with client isolation enabled (guest networks do this) all look the same. `arp -an` shows whether the gateway's MAC was ever learned: `(incomplete)` means nobody answered the ARP request.
DNS-only failure

`ping 1.1.1.1` works, `ping example.com` says `cannot resolve example.com: Unknown host`. Run `scutil --dns | head -20` to see which servers macOS asks, then `dig @1.1.1.1 +short example.com`. If the direct query works, the configured resolver is dead or blocked: switch the resolver (a public one or the router's) or flush the cache.

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 1 example.com
ping: cannot resolve example.com: Unknown host
$ ping -c 1 1.1.1.1 | tail -2
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 11.7/11.7/11.7/0.0 ms
$ dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 @1.1.1.1 example.com
93.184.216.34
$ scutil --dns | grep -m2 nameserver
  nameserver[0] : 192.0.2.53

blocks.text: Here the Mac asks `192.0.2.53`, a resolver that is gone, while a public resolver answers fine.
TLS errors

`curl: (60) SSL certificate problem` or a browser warning. The usual causes, in order of frequency: the Mac's clock is wrong (check `date`; certificates have validity dates), the site's certificate really expired, or something in the path intercepts TLS (a corporate proxy, antivirus, a hotel portal). `curl -v` prints the certificate chain being checked; `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer` shows who issued the certificate and when it expires. An unexpected issuer name on a site you know points to interception.
Captive portal

Hotels, airports and cafes allow the association and DHCP but intercept web traffic until you log in. Everything below HTTP looks healthy, which makes it confusing. Apple's own probe is a plain HTTP page:

blocks.code:
$ curl -s -m 5 http://captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html
<HTML><HEAD><TITLE>Success</TITLE></HEAD><BODY>Success</BODY></HTML>
$ curl -s -m 5 http://captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html | head -c 120
<html><head><meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0;url=https://login.cafe-wifi.example/portal"></head></html>

blocks.text: Anything other than the `Success` page, usually a redirect or a login form, means a portal is in the way. Open `http://neverssl.com` in a browser to trigger the login page. It is a plain HTTP site on purpose: a portal can redirect HTTP to its login page, while a redirect of HTTPS traffic shows up as a certificate error, which is also what `curl` reports on such networks.
Slow only on Wi-Fi

Wired is fast, Wi-Fi is slow or drops: measure the radio. `system_profiler SPAirPortDataType` lists the current channel, signal and noise; the gap between them is your **signal-to-noise ratio**, and under about 25 dB streaming gets unreliable.

blocks.code:
$ system_profiler SPAirPortDataType | grep -A8 'Current Network Information'
          Current Network Information:
            HomeNet:
              PHY Mode: 802.11ax
              Channel: 36 (5GHz, 80MHz)
              Country Code: US
              Network Type: Infrastructure
              Security: WPA2 Personal
              Signal / Noise: -61 dBm / -92 dBm
              Transmit Rate: 866

blocks.text: `-61 / -92` is a 31 dB gap, fine. `-78 / -90` is 12 dB, poor: move closer, change channel, or use 5 GHz. `networkQuality` (built in since macOS 12) measures throughput and responsiveness against Apple servers and shows whether the link or the congestion is the limit.
An MTU black hole

Small things work (ping, DNS, the start of a page) but large transfers hang: sites load their text and stall on images, SSH connects and freezes when output scrolls. A tunnel or PPPoE link has a smaller MTU than 1500, and a device in the path drops oversized packets without telling you. Probe with the Don't Fragment bit and shrink the payload until it passes:

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1472 1.1.1.1
PING 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1): 1472 data bytes
ping: sendto: Message too long
$ ping -c 1 -D -s 1452 1.1.1.1 | tail -2
1 packets transmitted, 1 packets received, 0.0% packet loss
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 14.1/14.1/14.1/0.0 ms

blocks.text: The largest payload that passes plus 28 bytes of headers (20 IP + 8 ICMP) is the path MTU: here 1452 + 28 = 1480. The usual fix lives in the router or tunnel (MSS clamping), not on the Mac.
Broken IPv6

Some sites hang for several seconds and then load; others fail only in some apps. The Mac has an IPv6 address and tries it first, but the router or ISP does not route IPv6 properly. Compare the families:

blocks.code:
curl -4 -sS -o /dev/null -m 8 -w 'v4 %{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com
curl -6 -sS -o /dev/null -m 8 -w 'v6 %{http_code} %{time_total}s\n' https://example.com

blocks.text: If `-4` is fast and `-6` fails or crawls, IPv6 is the culprit. Browsers hide some of the delay with a technique called Happy Eyeballs (try both and use the winner), but not all programs do. Test with IPv6 off for one service (`networksetup -setv6off Wi-Fi`, undo with `-setv6automatic`) and fix it at the router.
VPN and split DNS

After connecting a VPN, internal names resolve but public sites break, or the reverse. VPN software adds **per-domain resolvers**: queries for `corp.example` go to the VPN's DNS server, everything else to the old one. `scutil --dns` lists them as numbered resolvers with `domain`, `nameserver` and `if_index`. Name lookups hang if a resolver on a vanished `utun` interface still has the default scope.

blocks.code:
$ scutil --dns | grep -E '^resolver|domain|nameserver|if_index'
resolver #1
  nameserver[0] : 192.168.1.1
  if_index : 15 (en0)
resolver #2
  domain   : corp.example
  nameserver[0] : 10.8.0.1
  if_index : 21 (utun4)

blocks.text: Queries for `*.corp.example` go to `10.8.0.1` through `utun4`; everything else goes to `192.168.1.1`. If `utun4` is gone and resolver #2 remains, disconnect and reconnect the VPN, or flush the cache.
Slow, not broken: localizing delay with curl

When something works but takes too long, the question changes from "which layer fails" to "which phase is slow". `curl -w` prints the elapsed time at each milestone of one request. The values are **cumulative** from the start, so you subtract neighbours to get the cost of each phase.

blocks.name: curl -w
blocks.sum: Print timing and status variables after a request finishes, to see where the time goes.

how.text: The `-w` (write-out) string is printed after the transfer, with `%{variable}` placeholders replaced. The timing variables are cumulative seconds since the request began: `time_namelookup` (DNS done), `time_connect` (TCP handshake done), `time_appconnect` (TLS handshake done, 0 for plain HTTP), `time_pretransfer` (ready to send), `time_starttransfer` (first byte of the response arrived) and `time_total`.

Subtracting neighbours gives the phases: DNS = `namelookup`; TCP = `connect - namelookup`; TLS = `appconnect - connect`; server wait = `starttransfer - appconnect`; download = `total - starttransfer`. The large value is where to look: DNS (resolver), TCP (path latency or loss), TLS (CPU or interception), wait (the application), download (bandwidth).

flags.d: Discard the body so only the `-w` text is printed.
Give up after this many seconds in total.
The write-out format; `\n` adds a newline.

examples.desc: Time the phases of one HTTPS request
examples.code: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'dns %{time_namelookup}  tcp %{time_connect}  tls %{time_appconnect}  ttfb %{time_starttransfer}  total %{time_total}\n' https://{{domain}}

examples.desc: Turn the cumulative values into per-phase milliseconds with awk
examples.code: curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}' https://{{domain}} | awk '{printf "dns %.0f  tcp %.0f  tls %.0f  wait %.0f  download %.0f (ms)\n", $1*1000, ($2-$1)*1000, ($3-$2)*1000, ($4-$3)*1000, ($5-$4)*1000}'

examples.desc: Show only the status code and a failure reason in a script

anat.exp: silent progress, but keep error messages
print the status code and total time after the transfer

gotchas: For `http://` URLs `time_appconnect` is 0, so the TLS subtraction goes negative. Check for 0 first.

blocks.code:
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}\n' https://example.com; done
0.004110 0.016420 0.047388 0.091233 0.091700
0.004025 0.015977 0.045911 0.088610 0.089004
5.012336 5.025188 5.058342 5.101219 5.101814

blocks.text: The third request lost five seconds in the very first column, before TCP started. That is a DNS timeout followed by a fallback to a second resolver. No amount of looking at the web server would have found it.
Fixes, from gentle to drastic
Try these in order; each one is a bigger hammer than the last. Commands that change system state are marked.

blocks.name: ipconfig set
blocks.sum: Force an interface to restart DHCP and request a new lease.

how.text: `ipconfig set en0 DHCP` tells the configuration daemon to drop the interface's current IPv4 configuration and start the DHCP exchange again (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge). It fixes a stale lease, a lease from the wrong network after moving between access points, and the 169.254 state once the DHCP server is reachable again. It needs root because it reconfigures an interface.

The read-only twin `ipconfig getpacket en0` prints the last DHCP reply: the router (`router`), DNS servers (`domain_name_server`), lease length and the DHCP server's own address (`server_identifier`).

examples.desc: See what the DHCP server handed out
Renew, wait, and print the new address
examples.code: sudo ipconfig set {{iface}} DHCP && sleep 3 && ipconfig getifaddr {{iface}}

gotchas: Briefly drops connectivity on that interface, so do not run it inside an SSH session that rides on it.

blocks.title: Renewing a lease disconnects you for a moment

blocks.text: Running `sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP` over an SSH session that uses `en0` can cut your own connection. Run it from the machine's local Terminal. If the address stays `169.254.x.x`, the problem is the router or the link, not the Mac.
Cycle the Wi-Fi radio, which forces a fresh association and DHCP exchange and clears most half-dead states:

blocks.code:
networksetup -setairportpower en0 off
sleep 3
networksetup -setairportpower en0 on

blocks.text: If you have a wired service too, disable and re-enable a whole network service (use the name that `networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder` prints):

blocks.code:
networksetup -listnetworkserviceorder
networksetup -setnetworkserviceenabled "Wi-Fi" off
networksetup -setnetworkserviceenabled "Wi-Fi" on

blocks.name: flush DNS cache
blocks.sum: Throw away cached DNS answers so the next lookup asks the network again.

how.text: macOS caches answers in `mDNSResponder` (the system's DNS and Bonjour daemon) and a small directory-services cache. After you change a DNS server, edit `/etc/hosts` or a record is updated upstream, a stale answer can survive until its TTL expires. The two commands clear the directory-services cache and send `mDNSResponder` the `HUP` signal, which makes it empty its cache. Neither restarts your network.
Flushing fixes only stale or poisoned cache entries. If the resolver itself is down, a flush changes nothing.

examples.desc: Flush and test the system resolver path
Confirm what the system resolver returns for a name
Compare the system resolver with a direct query
examples.code: diff <(dscacheutil -q host -a name {{domain}} | awk '/^ip_address:/ {print $2}' | sort) <(dig +short @1.1.1.1 {{domain}} | sort)

gotchas: Both commands are needed; there is no single supported "flush" command on current macOS. There is no output on success.

blocks.name: route flush
blocks.sum: Delete all gateway routes from the routing table so they are rebuilt.

how.text: `route flush` removes every route that goes through a gateway. Local-subnet routes and the loopback route come back by themselves, and the default route is re-added when the network service reconfigures (a DHCP renewal or reconnecting Wi-Fi does it). It is a last resort for a table that holds a stale or wrong route, such as after a VPN crashed and left a route into a dead tunnel. `-n` prints addresses numerically instead of resolving names.

examples.desc: Show the table, flush, and look again
examples.code:
netstat -rn | head -12
sudo route -n flush
netstat -rn | head -12

gotchas: Right after the flush you have no default route, so every connection stops until the network service rebuilds it. Renew DHCP or toggle Wi-Fi straight away.

blocks.title: route flush cuts your own connection

blocks.text: Never run `sudo route -n flush` over SSH to a remote machine: the default route vanishes and your session dies with no way back in. Run it on the local console, and have `sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP` ready to type.

Check whether a proxy is silently in the path. Browsers follow the system proxy settings; `curl` ignores them and only reads environment variables such as `https_proxy`, so "curl works, Safari does not" often means a proxy or an auto-config (PAC) file is involved.

blocks.name: scutil --proxy
blocks.sum: Show the proxy settings the system currently applies.

how.text: `scutil --proxy` prints the merged proxy configuration as a dictionary: `HTTPEnable`, `HTTPProxy`, `HTTPPort`, the HTTPS and SOCKS equivalents, `ProxyAutoConfigEnable` with a `ProxyAutoConfigURLString` for PAC files, and an `ExceptionsList` of hosts that bypass the proxy. A value of `1` for an `...Enable` key means it is switched on. `networksetup -getwebproxy Wi-Fi` shows the per-service view.

examples.desc: List only the switched-on proxy kinds
Check whether the shell environment sets proxies for curl

blocks.name: wdutil
blocks.sum: Print a detailed report on the current Wi-Fi connection (signal, noise, channel, rates).

how.text: `wdutil` is the command-line side of Wireless Diagnostics (it replaced the removed `airport` utility). `info` prints sections for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread and the network: RSSI (signal strength in dBm), noise, transmit rate, channel and width, security and the interface's addresses. RSSI close to 0 is stronger: `-50` is excellent, `-70` marginal, `-80` unusable. Subtract the noise figure to get the signal-to-noise ratio.
Recent macOS versions redact the SSID, BSSID and MAC address in this report, but the radio measurements still print.

examples.desc: Pull out just the radio numbers

gotchas: Needs sudo. Field names can change between macOS releases, so print the whole report once and check the labels before scripting it.

blocks.name: nc -vz
blocks.sum: Test whether a TCP port accepts connections, without sending any data.

how.text: `nc` (netcat) opens a TCP connection. `-z` means "zero I/O": connect, report, close, send nothing. `-v` prints the result. `-w` bounds the wait, which matters because a firewall that drops packets would otherwise leave you waiting for the system timeout. The exit status is 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so it works in `if` and `&&`.

Read the failure type: an immediate `Connection refused` means the host is up and nothing listens on the port; a timeout after `-w` seconds means the packets are being dropped or the host is unreachable.

examples.desc: Check several ports and print only the ones that open
examples.code: for p in 22 80 443 8080; do nc -z -w 2 {{host}} $p && echo "$p open"; done

anat.exp: scan only: connect and close, no data

gotchas: Only scan hosts you own or have permission to test, such as your own machines or `scanme.nmap.org`.

blocks.name: ping -D
blocks.sum: Send pings with the Don't Fragment bit set to find the largest packet a path will carry.

how.text: `-s` sets the ICMP payload size and `-D` sets the Don't Fragment (DF) bit, so a router that cannot forward the packet whole must drop it instead of splitting it. A standard Ethernet MTU of 1500 bytes minus 20 bytes of IP header and 8 bytes of ICMP header leaves a payload of 1472. If 1472 fails and a smaller size passes, the path MTU is smaller than 1500, and the largest passing payload plus 28 is that MTU.
When the failure comes from your own interface, ping prints `Message too long` at once. When a router in the path drops the packet silently, you get timeouts, which is the black-hole case.

examples.desc: Find the path MTU by trying decreasing sizes
examples.code: for s in 1472 1452 1432 1400 1372; do ping -c 1 -t 2 -D -s $s {{host}} >/dev/null 2>&1 && { echo "payload $s passes, MTU $((s+28))"; break; }; done

gotchas: Some networks block ICMP, which looks like an MTU problem. Confirm that a small ping to the same host works first.

blocks.text: Project: netdoctor.zsh

blocks.title: netdoctor.zsh, a diagnosis that stops at the broken layer

blocks.text: `netcheck.zsh` ([Scripting](#scripting)) reports six results and keeps going. `netdoctor.zsh` is smarter about order: it tests bottom-up, stops climbing when a layer fails (the layers above would only fail for the same reason), distinguishes warnings from failures, and ends with a short list of suggested fixes. The exit status is the number of failures, so it still works in cron and launchd.

blocks.code:
link ─▶ address ─▶ gateway ─▶ internet ─▶ DNS ─▶ portal ─▶ TCP ─▶ HTTPS ─▶ extras
     │        │          │           │                                          │
     └────────┴──────────┴───────────┘                                          └─ MTU, IPv6, proxy
        a FAIL here stops the climb:                                               (warnings only)
        higher tests would only repeat the failure

blocks.text: Step 1: Skeleton, helpers and the fix list
Create `~/bin/netdoctor.zsh`. The helpers `ok`, `warn` and `bad` print a coloured line; `bad` also stores a suggested fix so the summary can list them.
The `${3:-}` form supplies an empty string when no third argument was passed. Without it, `NO_UNSET` would abort the script on the first `ok` call that omits the fix.
Step 2: The lower layers
Each check returns 0 to continue and 1 to stop the climb. Warnings return 0 because the layer is usable.

blocks.code:
check_link() {
  iface=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/interface:/ {print $2}')
  if [[ -z $iface ]]; then
    bad "default route" "none" "Join a network, or cycle Wi-Fi: networksetup -setairportpower en0 off; networksetup -setairportpower en0 on"
    return 1
  fi
  local st
  st=$(ifconfig $iface 2>/dev/null | awk '/status:/ {print $2}')
  if [[ $st == inactive ]]; then
    bad "link $iface" "inactive" "Check the cable or rejoin Wi-Fi"
    return 1
  fi
  ok "link $iface" "${st:-up}"
}

check_address() {
  myip=$(ipconfig getifaddr $iface 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ -z $myip ]]; then
    bad "address" "$iface has no IPv4 address" "sudo ipconfig set $iface DHCP"
    return 1
  elif [[ $myip == 169.254.* ]]; then
    bad "address" "$myip (link-local, DHCP failed)" "sudo ipconfig set $iface DHCP, then check the router's DHCP server"
    return 1
  fi
  ok "address" "$myip"
}

check_gateway() {
  gw=$(route -n get default 2>/dev/null | awk '/gateway:/ {print $2}')
  [[ -n $gw ]] || { ok "gateway" "none (point-to-point link)"; return 0 }
  local out loss avg
  out=$(ping -c 4 -t 6 $gw 2>/dev/null)
  loss=$(print -r -- "$out" | awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}')
  avg=$(print -r -- "$out" | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {printf "%.1f", $5}')
  loss=${loss%\%}
  if [[ -z $loss || $loss == 100.0 ]]; then
    bad "gateway $gw" "no reply" "Wrong network or router down: power-cycle the router, then run: arp -an | grep $gw"
    return 1
  elif (( loss > 0 )); then
    warn "gateway $gw" "${loss}% loss, ${avg} ms" "Weak or noisy link: move closer, try 5 GHz, run: networkQuality"
  else
    ok "gateway $gw" "${avg} ms"
  fi
}

check_internet() {
  local out loss avg
  out=$(ping -c 3 -t 5 1.1.1.1 2>/dev/null)
  loss=$(print -r -- "$out" | awk '/packet loss/ {print $7}')
  avg=$(print -r -- "$out" | awk -F/ '/round-trip/ {printf "%.1f", $5}')
  if [[ -z $loss || ${loss%\%} == 100.0 ]]; then
    bad "internet 1.1.1.1" "no reply" "Gateway works but nothing beyond it: check the modem and ISP, then: traceroute -n 1.1.1.1"
    return 1
  fi
  ok "internet 1.1.1.1" "${avg} ms"
}

blocks.text: The `loss` field comes from the macOS statistics line `3 packets transmitted, 3 packets received, 0.0% packet loss`, whose seventh whitespace-separated word is `0.0%`. When ping cannot even send, there is no statistics line, `loss` is empty, and the empty test catches it.

blocks.title: Quote what you feed to awk

blocks.text: `print -r -- "$out"` keeps the multi-line ping output intact. zsh does not word-split an unquoted `$out` by default, but bash and sh do: there `echo $out` joins the words into one long line, so the `/packet loss/` pattern would still match but field numbers would shift. Quoting is correct in every shell.
Step 3: Name resolution, portal, transport and application
This is the half that separates the failure types. The DNS check asks twice, once through the system resolver and once straight to `1.1.1.1`, because the *combination* of answers is the diagnosis.

blocks.code:
check_dns() {
  local sys direct
  sys=$(dscacheutil -q host -a name $domain 2>/dev/null | awk '/^ip_address:/ {print $2; exit}')
  direct=$(dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 @1.1.1.1 $domain A 2>/dev/null | grep -E '^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$' | head -1)
  if [[ -n $sys ]]; then
    ok "DNS $domain" "$sys"
  elif [[ -n $direct ]]; then
    bad "DNS $domain" "system resolver fails, 1.1.1.1 answers ($direct)" "Your DNS server is dead: networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi ; flush with: sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder"
    return 1
  else
    bad "DNS $domain" "no answer from any resolver" "UDP/53 may be blocked: try another network, or ask whether $domain exists"
    return 1
  fi
}

check_portal() {
  local body
  body=$(curl -s -m 5 http://captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html 2>/dev/null)
  if [[ $body == *Success* ]]; then
    ok "captive portal" "none"
  else
    warn "captive portal" "probe page altered or empty" "Open http://neverssl.com in a browser and log in to the network's portal"
  fi
}

check_tcp() {
  local port=443 h=${${url#*://}%%[/:]*}
  if nc -z -w 5 $h $port 2>/dev/null; then
    ok "tcp $h:$port" "open"
  else
    bad "tcp $h:$port" "cannot connect" "Firewall or host down: test another site; if only this one fails, the fault is on its side"
    return 1
  fi
}

check_https() {
  local out rc code dns con tls ttfb tot
  out=$(curl -sS -o /dev/null -m 8 -w '%{http_code} %{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_appconnect} %{time_starttransfer} %{time_total}' $url 2>/dev/null)
  rc=$?
  case $rc in
    0) ;;
    6)  bad "HTTP $url" "curl 6: could not resolve host" "See the DNS result above"; return 1 ;;
    7)  bad "HTTP $url" "curl 7: connection failed" "Port closed or blocked"; return 1 ;;
    28) bad "HTTP $url" "curl 28: timed out" "Server or path too slow: run the curl -w timing loop"; return 1 ;;
    35|60) bad "HTTP $url" "curl $rc: TLS problem" "Check the clock with date, then: openssl s_client -connect ${${url#*://}%%/*}:443 -servername ${${url#*://}%%/*} </dev/null"; return 1 ;;
    *)  bad "HTTP $url" "curl exit $rc" "Run: curl -v $url"; return 1 ;;
  esac
  set -- ${=out}
  code=$1 dns=$2 con=$3 tls=$4 ttfb=$5 tot=$6
  (( tls > 0 )) || tls=$con
  local d t s w
  d=$(( dns * 1000 )) t=$(( (con - dns) * 1000 )) s=$(( (tls - con) * 1000 )) w=$(( (ttfb - tls) * 1000 ))
  if [[ $code == [23]* ]]; then
    ok "HTTP $url" "$code in $(printf '%.0f' $(( tot * 1000 ))) ms (dns $(printf '%.0f' $d), tcp $(printf '%.0f' $t), tls $(printf '%.0f' $s), wait $(printf '%.0f' $w))"
  else
    warn "HTTP $url" "status $code" "The server answered with an error: it is the service, not your network"
  fi
}

blocks.text: `${${url#*://}%%[/:]*}` strips the scheme (`https://`), then everything from the first `/` or `:` onward, leaving the bare host. `set -- ${=out}` splits the curl output on whitespace (the `=` forces word splitting in zsh) into `$1`...`$6`.
Step 4: Extras, summary and the run order
The extras are warnings only: they point at problems that cause *slowness*, not outages.

blocks.code:
check_extras() {
  # path MTU: full-size DF packet
  if ! ping -c 1 -t 3 -D -s 1472 1.1.1.1 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    warn "path MTU" "1500-byte packets do not pass" "Find the limit with ping -D -s; fix MSS or MTU on the router or tunnel"
  fi
  # IPv6: only test when a global address exists
  if ifconfig $iface 2>/dev/null | grep -Eq 'inet6 [23]'; then
    if ! curl -6 -s -o /dev/null -m 5 $url 2>/dev/null; then
      warn "IPv6" "global address but curl -6 fails" "Disable IPv6 for the service or fix it on the router: networksetup -setv6off Wi-Fi"
    fi
  fi
  # system proxy
  if scutil --proxy 2>/dev/null | grep -Eq '(HTTP|HTTPS|ProxyAutoConfig)Enable : 1'; then
    warn "proxy" "a system proxy is enabled" "Browsers use it, curl does not: scutil --proxy"
  fi
}

check_link && check_address && check_gateway && check_internet &&
  check_dns && { check_portal; check_tcp && check_https && check_extras }

print
if (( fails )); then
  print "Diagnosis: $fails failure(s), $warns warning(s). Start with the first FAIL above."
elif (( warns )); then
  print "Working, with $warns warning(s)."
else
  print "All layers healthy."
fi
if (( ${#fixes} )); then
  print "Suggested next steps:"
  for f in $fixes; do print "  - $f"; done
fi
exit $(( fails > 255 ? 255 : fails ))

blocks.text: The chain `a && b && c && ...` is the whole stop-at-first-failure logic: each `check_*` returns non-zero after printing its FAIL, and `&&` skips everything after it. The braces group the last four checks so `check_portal` runs but cannot stop the climb.

tokens.exp: layer 1-2: returns 1 after printing a FAIL
run the next test only if the previous returned 0
needs a link to mean anything
the climb stops at the first test that returns non-zero
never runs if a lower layer failed

blocks.code:
$ netdoctor.zsh
[ OK ] link en0             active
[ OK ] address              192.168.1.23
[ OK ] gateway 192.168.1.1  2.8 ms
[ OK ] internet 1.1.1.1     12.0 ms
[FAIL] DNS example.com      system resolver fails, 1.1.1.1 answers (93.184.216.34)

Diagnosis: 1 failure(s), 0 warning(s). Start with the first FAIL above.
Suggested next steps:
  - Your DNS server is dead: networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi ; flush with: sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder
$ echo $?
1

blocks.text: Run `netdoctor.zsh` on a healthy network and confirm it ends with `All layers healthy.` Then reproduce each fault in turn: turn Wi-Fi off (link or route fails first), run it with `-d does-not-exist.invalid` (DNS fails, lower layers stay green), run it with `-u https://expired.badssl.com` (TLS failure with curl exit 60). Each fault should stop the walk at a different layer. If one does not, your script has a bug worth finding.

Add a `-v` flag that prints the raw command output behind each check. Add a check that your DNS servers from `scutil --dns` respond. Append a timestamped one-line summary to `~/netdoctor.log` on every run and schedule it with launchd (see [Scripting](#scripting)), so you have evidence the next time the network misbehaves "sometimes".
Case studies
Read each transcript before looking at the explanation. Name the failing layer from the output alone.
Case 1: "Everything is down"

blocks.code:
$ ifconfig en0 | grep -E 'status|inet '
	inet 169.254.87.201 netmask 0xffff0000 broadcast 169.254.255.255
	status: active
$ ping -c 2 -t 4 1.1.1.1
ping: sendto: No route to host
ping: sendto: No route to host

blocks.text: The link is active and an address exists, so the radio is fine. The address is `169.254.x.x`: DHCP failed, so there is no default route and `1.1.1.1` cannot be reached. The layer is **address**. Renew the lease; if it stays link-local, look at the router's DHCP pool.
Case 2: "Google loads but my work site does not"

blocks.code:
$ ping -c 2 intranet.corp.example
ping: cannot resolve intranet.corp.example: Unknown host
$ dig +short intranet.corp.example
$ dig +short @10.8.0.1 intranet.corp.example
10.8.4.20
$ scutil --dns | grep -B1 -A3 'corp.example'

blocks.text: The VPN's DNS server answers when asked directly, but the system resolver has no entry that sends `corp.example` queries there (the last command printed nothing). The layer is **name resolution**, specifically split DNS: the VPN connected but did not install its per-domain resolver. Reconnect the VPN client; if it persists, the client needs "use VPN DNS for these domains" configured.
Case 3: "Pages load slowly, then fine"

blocks.code:
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{time_namelookup} %{time_connect} %{time_total}\n' https://example.com; done
0.004 0.017 0.092
5.011 5.026 5.102
0.004 0.017 0.090
$ ping -c 3 192.168.1.1 | tail -1
round-trip min/avg/max/stddev = 2.1/2.6/3.2/0.4 ms

blocks.text: The gateway is fast, TCP and TLS are fast, and the whole delay sits in the first column on the second run: five seconds of DNS. The first resolver timed out (the usual per-server timeout) and the second answered. The layer is **name resolution**, and the cause is a dead resolver in the list. `networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi` shows the list; remove the dead entry.
Practice

blocks.title: Name the layer

task.text: For each symptom, name the *first* layer you would test and the command you would use, then say what result would send you up or down.

items.text: A website opens on your phone's cellular data but not over home Wi-Fi.
`nc -vz -w 5 example.com 443` returns `Connection refused` immediately; the same command to port 8443 hangs for five seconds and times out.

hints: For each one ask which test splits the stack in half.
blocks.solution:
1. Both devices reach the internet, so test from the Mac on the same Wi-Fi: `curl -sv` that site. A DNS answer that differs from the phone's, or a connection that stalls, points at DNS or the path. Compare `dig +short site` with `dig +short @1.1.1.1 site`.
2. The IP layer is healthy; the fault is name resolution. Run `dig +short @1.1.1.1 dns.google` and `scutil --dns` to find which resolver fails.
3. Port 443 answered with a reset: the host is up and nothing listens there (or a firewall actively rejects). Port 8443 gave no answer: packets are being dropped, a firewall policy or a dead service on a host that silently ignores closed ports. Refused is a fast "no", timeout is silence.

why.text: The skill is choosing the test that eliminates the most layers at once. A number-based test removes DNS; a name-based test of a second resolver isolates the resolver; refused versus timed out separates a host that is alive from a path that is not.

blocks.title: Read the lease

task.text: `ipconfig getifaddr en0` prints `169.254.12.4`. Your housemate's laptop on the same Wi-Fi works normally. List three things that could be wrong, and the command that would narrow each down.

hints: DHCP is a four-step conversation; any step can fail.
blocks.solution:
- Your Mac's request never reached the server or the reply never came back: a weak or flapping link. Check `ifconfig en0 | grep status` and `sudo wdutil info` for RSSI/noise, then `sudo ipconfig set en0 DHCP`.
- The DHCP server has no free leases or is not running: the other laptop already has a lease, so ask the router. `ipconfig getpacket en0` would show a past reply if there was one.
- The router restricts clients by MAC address and your Mac uses a private (randomized) Wi-Fi address that is not allowed. Compare `ifconfig en0 | grep ether` with the router's allow-list, or set the network's Private Wi-Fi Address option to Off in System Settings.

why.text: A link-local address means one specific thing: DHCP did not complete. Working devices on the same network narrow it to your Mac or your connection to the access point.

blocks.title: Split a slow request

task.text: A curl write-out line has five cumulative times: `time_namelookup time_connect time_appconnect time_starttransfer time_total`. Write `phases(line)` that returns a dict with the milliseconds spent in `dns`, `tcp`, `tls`, `wait` and `download`, rounded to whole numbers. If `time_appconnect` is 0 (plain HTTP), make `tls` 0 and measure `wait` from `time_connect`.

why.text: The timing variables are running totals, so each phase is the difference between neighbours. Handling the zero `time_appconnect` is the same guard `netdoctor.zsh` uses. Rounding after multiplying avoids float noise such as 12.999999.

blocks.title: Break DNS, then fix it

task.text: Record your current DNS servers, point Wi-Fi at a dead server, watch the system resolver fail while a direct query to a public resolver still works, then restore the original setting. Use `Wi-Fi` or the service name that `networksetup -listallnetworkservices` shows.

hints: `networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi` prints the current list, or a message saying none are set (you use the DHCP-provided ones).
`networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi Empty` clears the manual list and restores the DHCP default.
blocks.solution:
networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi
sudo networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi 192.0.2.53
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder
ping -c 1 -t 3 example.com
dig +short +time=2 +tries=1 @1.1.1.1 example.com
sudo networksetup -setdnsservers Wi-Fi Empty
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder
ping -c 1 -t 3 example.com

why.text: `192.0.2.53` is in a documentation range that nothing answers, so the system resolver times out while `dig @1.1.1.1` proves the internet is fine: the exact signature of a dead resolver. If you had a manual DNS list before, put those addresses back instead of `Empty`.

blocks.verify: networksetup -getdnsservers Wi-Fi; ping -c 1 -t 3 example.com > /dev/null && echo "OK: name resolution restored"

blocks.title: Catch the portal

task.text: Without a browser, decide whether the network you are on is intercepting web traffic. Fetch Apple's probe page and print `portal` or `clear` depending on whether the body contains `Success`.

hints: `curl -s -m 5 URL` prints the body. `grep -q` sets the exit status without printing.
blocks.solution: curl -s -m 5 http://captive.apple.com/hotspot-detect.html | grep -q Success && echo clear || echo portal

why.text: Operating systems detect portals exactly this way: fetch a known page over plain HTTP and compare. A portal replaces the page with a redirect or a login form. Note `a && b || c` prints `portal` when the fetch fails as well, which is reasonable here because a failed probe also means no usable internet.

questions.q: You can ping 1.1.1.1 but not example.com. Which layer is the first suspect?
questions.why: A reply from an IP address proves the link, address, gateway and internet path all work. Only the name lookup is left.

questions.q: What does an address of 169.254.87.201 on en0 tell you?

options.text: The router assigned a private address
DHCP failed and macOS gave itself a link-local address
The interface is a VPN tunnel

questions.why: 169.254.0.0/16 is the link-local range a host self-assigns when no DHCP server answers.

questions.q: `nc -vz example.com 8443` fails instantly with "Connection refused". What does that mean?

options.text: A firewall silently dropped the packets
The host answered and nothing is listening on that port

questions.why: A refusal is a TCP reset sent by a live host. A silent drop produces a timeout instead.

questions.q: In `curl -w`, why do you subtract `time_connect` from `time_appconnect`?

options.text: The timing values are cumulative, so the difference is the TLS handshake time

questions.why: Every `time_*` value counts from the start of the request. Differences between neighbours give each phase.

questions.q: Which `ping` flags, used together, test whether a 1500-byte path MTU works end to end?
questions.why: `-D` sets Don't Fragment and `-s 1472` plus 28 header bytes makes a 1500-byte packet.

questions.q: `dig example.com` works but Safari cannot load the site, and `curl` works. What should you check next?

options.text: The system proxy settings (`scutil --proxy`) and per-domain resolvers (`scutil --dns`)

questions.why: dig and curl bypass the system proxy and, for dig, the macOS resolver. Browsers use both, so a proxy, PAC file or split-DNS entry can break only them.

blocks.text: Glossary and next steps

Next: [Python: getting started](#py-start) begins the Python part of the book, where you will rebuild these tools in a language that handles structure, errors and data far better than shell scripts do.

terms.def: A self-assigned 169.254.x.x IPv4 address a host uses when DHCP fails; it only works on the local segment
The routing entry used when no more specific route matches; its gateway is the way out of the local network
A network that intercepts web traffic until you log in or accept terms
Sending queries for some domains to one resolver and everything else to another, as VPNs often do
The largest packet that crosses an entire path without fragmentation
A path that silently drops packets larger than some size, so small traffic works and large transfers stall
A client technique that tries IPv6 and IPv4 almost together and uses whichever connects first
A proxy auto-config script a browser downloads to decide which proxy, if any, each URL uses
Received signal strength indicator, in dBm; closer to 0 is stronger
Signal strength minus noise floor in dB; a bigger gap means a cleaner Wi-Fi link
curl's cumulative time until the TLS handshake finished
An immediate TCP reset: the host is up and nothing listens on that port
